Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at Example 1 (2025-04-09):
- History: Prices have been declining from ~71.30 to ~62.06 over 18 days
- Sentiment: Mixed, ending at 0.33
- Model forecasts: Start at 61.48 and gradually increase to ~68.91
- True outcomes: Start at 60.94 and gradually increase to ~72.15

The model is too low compared to true outcomes. The true outcomes are about 2-4 points higher than forecasts.

Example 2 (2024-09-17):
- History: Prices declining from ~71.57 to ~63.21
- Sentiment: Various, ending at 0.67
- Model forecasts: Start at 64.86, end at 69.32
- True outcomes: Start at 64.34, end at 66.97

In this case, model forecasts are slightly higher than true outcomes (by about 1-3 points).

Example 3 (2024-05-03):
- History: Prices more volatile, ending at ~72.69
- Sentiment: Various
- Model forecasts: Start at 72.13, end at 69.13
- True outcomes: Start at 71.84, end at 70.30

Model forecasts are slightly higher than true outcomes by about 1-3 points.

Example 4 (2024-05-02):
- History is almost identical to Example 3 (first 18 points)
- Sentiment varies
- Model forecasts: Start at 72.92, end at 71.33
- True outcomes: Start at 72.69, end at 70.30


- Model forecasts are about 1-3 points higher

I notice a consistent pattern emerging. When sentiment is positive (above 0.50), the model tends to underpredict prices by 2-4 points. Conversely, when sentiment is neutral or negative, the model overpredicts by 1-3 points. The differences appear to correlate with sentiment levels, suggesting a systematic bias in the forecasting model.
